title: Wildfire smoke, indoor and outdoor PM2.5, and sick-related absenteeism in Oklahoma Head Start early care and education centers - Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology
description: Wildfire smoke can infiltrate early care and education (ECE) buildings, yet evidence remains limited for children from birth to age 5, non-Western U.S. regions, and smoke-mitigation strategies in childcare classrooms. We examined wildfire smoke, indoor and outdoor PM2.5, and sick-related absenteeism in Oklahoma Head Start Centers. We analyzed Cohort 1 of the OK-AIR cluster-randomized 2×2 factorial trial, including 5 centers, 20 classrooms, and 204 children during 2023–2024. Classrooms were randomized to control, portable HEPA filtration, upper-room ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI), or HEPA + UVGI. Indoor PM2.5 was monitored continuously and paired with hourly EPA outdoor PM2.5. Wildfire smoke-impacted and non-impacted days during February-March 2024 were identified using NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke plumes. Indoor-outdoor PM2.5 relationships during smoke-impacted days were modeled using ordinary least squares regression. This analysis compared pooled Baseline and Intervention periods rather than arm-specific effects. Sick-related absenteeism was modeled across 4 centers and 16 classrooms using a binomial generalized linear model with a 7-day rolling average of the NASA FIRMS/VIIRS regional fire-detection metric. Indoor PM2.5 was higher on smoke-impacted days than on non-impacted days. After adjustment for outdoor PM2.5, the intervention-period indicator was associated with 29.0% lower indoor PM2.5 during smoke-impacted days (95% CI: 22.8–34.7%), and this contrast did not isolate HEPA, UVGI, or their combination. Each 100-detection increase in the 7-day rolling mean of regional fire detections was associated with higher odds of sick-related absence (OR = 1.106, 95% CI: 1.018–1.201, p = 0.018). The wildfire-by-period interaction was imprecise, and the data were insufficient to detect or exclude meaningful effect modification. Wildfire smoke was associated with higher indoor PM2.5, and regional wildfire activity was associated with sick-related absenteeism. Lower PM2.5 during Intervention periods was consistent with a possible contribution from filtration, but the period-based analysis did not estimate an arm-specific HEPA effect.
